body:
I love that you're helping! I don't know much about the internals of Godot, but I found this issue interesting and thought I might be able to help out.

Did you know there are tests in [`tests/core/math/test_math_func.h`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2d9ac2d98dd0b136a192e3617a15ad678fb458de/tests/core/math/test_math_funcs.h#L314-L338)? The can help out with this.

I whipped up some test cases based on the numbers you gave and the `main` branch failed on:

- `0.2500000000` (got 1, expected 2)
- `0.1250000000` (got 1, expected 3)
- `0.0000002500` (got 7, expected 8)

I then went to your branch, patched in my extra tests and ran it and got even more failures.

Looking at those three tests, I don't think they failed.

The decimal that is returned (though there isn't any good doc strings on the function) is the place of the first non-zero digit.

e.g., `0.1` returns `1` and `0.001` returns `3`. For some reason my brain thinks of it as "number of zeros after the decimal point, plus 1". I don't know why my brain thinks that way.

If that is what the function is meant to do, then it is working as advertised.

However, I agree that this may not be the expected way the editor inspector works. I suspect that the inspector code is going to need a string based float parser to get the results we expect.

 	CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.0) == 16);
 	CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)-0.5) == 16);
+	SUBCASE("Bug #95725") {
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.5000000000) == 1);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.2500000000) == 2);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.1250000000) == 3);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.0100000000) == 2);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.0050000000) == 3);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.0001000000) == 4);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.0000001000) == 7);
+		CHECK(Math::range_step_decimals((T)0.0000002500) == 8);
+	}
 }

PS: I think the reason your code is failing is because you're multiplying the float by 10 and removing the integer part.

Except these are IEEE floating numbers and the multiplication will introduce tiny values in the resulting number that are bigger than EPSILON and there for don't trip your check.

Basically, the multiplication is just amplifying the noise in the fractional part.
